A.io: 4e — Macrolides/ketolides
A.q: How do macrolides interact with other drugs, and in what order of severity?
opts: They chelate divalent cations, reducing absorption of co-administered drugs
Chelation is the tetracycline and fluoroquinolone interaction.
They displace substrates from plasma protein binding sites
Protein displacement is not the mechanism given.

Metabolites bind CYP3A subclass enzymes forming an inactive complex, raising levels of substrates such as carbamazepine, cyclosporine, digoxin, midazolam and theophylline, with erythromycin greater than clarithromycin greater than azithromycin
Correct. The ranking is the practical point: azithromycin is the one to reach for when interactions matter.

They induce CYP3A subclass enzymes, lowering levels of substrates such as carbamazepine, cyclosporine, digoxin, midazolam and theophylline, with azithromycin greater than clarithromycin greater than erythromycin
The effect is inhibition through an inactive complex, not induction, and azithromycin is the weakest.

A.io: 9b — Polyenes
A.q: From what source is amphotericin B derived?
opts: Penicillium griseofulvum
That is the source of griseofulvin.
Bacillus polymyxa
That is the source of the polymyxins, which are antibacterial.
The soil bacterium Amycolatopsis orientalis
That organism produces vancomycin.
A soil Streptomycetaceae organism
Correct, which places it alongside several antibacterials in being a natural product of a soil microbe.

A.io: 4c — Monobactams
A.q: What is the defining clinical advantage of aztreonam?
opts: No cross-reactivity with beta-lactams, so it can be used in truly penicillin-allergic patients
Correct. That property is what makes a monobactam worth having despite its narrow Gram-negative-only spectrum.
The broadest spectrum of any beta-lactam, covering Gram-positives, Gram-negatives and anaerobes
Aztreonam has only Gram-negative coverage, with no Gram-positive or anaerobic activity at all.
Oral bioavailability allowing outpatient completion of therapy
It is given intravenously, 1 to 2 grams every 8 hours.
Reliable central nervous system penetration for meningitis
Central nervous system penetration is highlighted for carbapenems and third generation cephalosporins.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: Why does the lecture counsel caution with dobutamine in atrial fibrillation?
opts: It causes bronchoconstriction
That is a beta blocker effect.
It depletes cardiac catecholamine stores
That is reserpine.
It increases atrioventricular conduction
Correct, which can accelerate the ventricular response.
It slows sinoatrial firing
It is a positive chronotrope.

A.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
A.q: Which retinoid does the lecture pair with Kaposi sarcoma?
opts: Adapalene
Adapalene is an acne agent notable for its stability.
Alitretinoin
Correct. Bexarotene is the one paired with T-cell lymphoma.
Bexarotene
Bexarotene is the retinoid the lecture links to T-cell lymphoma.
Tazarotene
Tazarotene is used for acne and psoriasis.

A.io: 4j — Glycopeptides & lipopeptides
A.q: When should a vancomycin trough be drawn?
opts: Immediately before the second dose
Levels drawn that early do not reflect steady state.
At any point within the dosing interval, provided the exact time of the draw is recorded
That flexibility applies to random levels in unstable renal function, not to routine troughs.
15 to 30 minutes before the next scheduled dose, usually around the third or fourth dose
Correct. Drawing around the third or fourth dose is what makes the level reflect steady state.
30 minutes after the end of the infusion
That is when a peak is drawn, and peaks are specified for the aminoglycosides.

A.io: 3 — Bacteriostatic versus bactericidal
A.q: What distinguishes a bacteriostatic drug from a bactericidal drug, as the lecture defines them?
opts: Bacteriostatic requires a higher concentration to act; bactericidal acts at any concentration above zero
Concentration matters for the pharmacodynamic classes, but it is not what separates static from cidal.
Bacteriostatic agents are given orally and bactericidal agents are given intravenously
Route is unrelated; penicillins are bactericidal and available orally, tetracyclines bacteriostatic and available intravenously.
Bacteriostatic inhibits a vital growth pathway without directly causing death; bactericidal disrupts function enough that death occurs
Correct. The lecture's split is about whether the drug itself kills, not about how fast it works.
Bacteriostatic works only on Gram-positive organisms; bactericidal works on both Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms
Spectrum and killing are independent properties; both categories in the lecture contain broad and narrow agents.

A.io: 6 — Anti-herpes agents
A.q: What does the lecture say about starting acyclovir within the first 24 hours of chickenpox?
opts: It cures the infection and prevents later reactivation as shingles
The lecture is explicit that it does not cure the infection.
It has no effect unless combined with valacyclovir
No such combination requirement is given.
It prevents transmission to contacts but does not alter the illness
The stated benefit is a shorter acute illness.
It shortens the acute illness but does not cure the infection
Correct — the virus is not eradicated, which is why reactivation as shingles remains possible later.

A.io: 3 — Classify the neurotransmitters released and the types of receptors found within the ANS
A.q: What does the lecture say norepinephrine acts as?
opts: Both a neurotransmitter and a hormone
Correct, and it also regulates normal brain processes, usually excitatory.
A neurotransmitter only, with no hormonal role
The lecture explicitly gives it both roles.
A hormone only, released from the adrenal cortex
It is a transmitter as well, and the adrenal medulla is the relevant gland.
An inhibitory transmitter in pain pathways of the spinal cord
That is serotonin.

A.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
A.q: What does the lecture say happens when epinephrine is given to a patient on a beta blocker?
opts: There is no clinically important interaction
The lecture lists it among the significant interactions.
Alpha effects are left unopposed
Correct. Blocking the vasodilating beta side leaves only vasoconstriction.
Both alpha and beta effects are abolished
The beta receptors are blocked; alpha remains available.
The blood pressure falls sharply
Unopposed alpha activity raises it.

A.io: 9b — Polyenes
A.q: Which electrolyte and renal effects accompany amphotericin B?
opts: Isolated hepatotoxicity with no renal involvement
Renal effects are the prominent ones for this agent.
Bone marrow suppression as the dose-limiting toxicity
Bone marrow suppression is the flucytosine concern.
Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, hypotension, uraemia in about 80 percent with decreased filtration, and renal tubule damage mitigated by hydration with normal saline
Correct. The saline hydration is the practical countermeasure worth remembering.
Hyperkalaemia and hypercalcaemia with a rising glomerular filtration rate, hypertension, and tubular hypertrophy that resolves without any need for hydration
The disturbances run in the opposite direction, and filtration falls rather than rises.

A.io: 8 — Anti-influenza agents
A.q: What route and dosing consideration apply to oseltamivir?
opts: Available intravenously only, with hepatic adjustment
It is an oral agent and the adjustment named is renal.
Available orally and intravenously, with no adjustment needed
It is oral only, and renal adjustment is required.
Available as an inhaled powder only
Inhaled administration is not described for this agent.
Available orally only, and requiring renal dose adjustment
Correct. Renal adjustment is a consideration rather than a dose to memorise.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: Which emergency indications does the lecture give for epinephrine?
opts: Hypertensive emergency
That is intravenous labetalol.
Chronic heart failure
That is dobutamine's territory.
Anaphylactic shock and cardiac arrest
Correct, alongside acute reversal of bronchospasm.
Cardiogenic and septic shock
Those are dopamine's indications.

A.io: 3 — Classify the neurotransmitters released and the types of receptors found within the ANS
A.q: How does the lecture characterise dopamine?
opts: Multiple functions by location, and usually inhibitory
Correct, which contrasts with acetylcholine being usually excitatory.
Purely excitatory, controlling muscle movement in spinal cord neurons
That is acetylcholine's description.
The major inhibitory transmitter of the brain
That is gamma-aminobutyric acid.
Involved chiefly in mood, appetite and sensory perception
That is serotonin.

A.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
A.q: Which of these is a LOCAL adverse effect of topical steroids in the lecture, rather than a systemic one?
opts: Adrenal suppression
This is on the lecture's systemic list.
Cataracts
Cataracts are listed as systemic, alongside glaucoma.
Growth retardation in children
This is a systemic effect in the lecture.
Skin atrophy
Correct. Local effects are skin atrophy, acne, rosacea and allergic dermatitis related to the vehicle.

A.io: 9 — Antifungal classes
A.q: How does flucytosine achieve selectivity for fungal cells?
opts: It is converted to 5-fluorouridine by cytosine deaminase, an enzyme human cells lack, and then inhibits thymidylate synthase
Correct. The missing human enzyme is the whole basis of selectivity.
It binds ergosterol, which human membranes do not contain
That selectivity argument belongs to the polyenes.
It inhibits a fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme with no human counterpart
That is closer to the azole mechanism, and human cytochrome P450 enzymes do exist, which is why azoles interact with other drugs.
It is actively pumped into fungal cells by a membrane transporter that is entirely absent from human cells and tissues
The lecture attributes selectivity to the converting enzyme, not to a transporter.

A.io: 9c — Azoles
A.q: Why is ketoconazole rarely used now?
opts: It does not enter the central nervous system and it inhibits cytochrome P450 3A4, producing significant drug interactions
Correct, and itraconazole with its wider spectrum largely replaced it.
It is available only intravenously and causes severe infusion reactions requiring routine premedication before every dose
Ketoconazole is oral, taken with meals, and also available topically.
It is the only azole ineffective against Candida
Its problems are penetration and interactions rather than a Candida gap.
It causes visual disturbance in about 30 percent of patients
That is voriconazole's characteristic effect.

A.io: 10 — Outline appropriate patient education for dermatologic drugs
A.q: Most topical acne agents cause skin irritation. What does the lecture say that leads to, and how does it advise starting?
opts: It confirms the drug is working, so maintain the starting strength
The lecture treats irritation as a barrier to adherence, not as a marker of efficacy.
It requires an immediate switch to systemic therapy, because irritation means the topical agent has failed
Severity, not irritation, is what moves a patient to systemic therapy.
It is prevented entirely by using an alcoholic solution
The lecture suggests considering non-alcoholic solutions, which is the reverse.
It can lead to patient discontinuation, so start with lower strength and increase gradually
Correct. Anticipating the irritation is what keeps a patient on therapy.

A.io: 4j — Glycopeptides & lipopeptides
A.q: What loading dose does the lecture give for vancomycin in critically ill patients?
opts: 15 to 20 milligrams per kilogram, rounded to the nearest 500 milligrams
That is the maintenance dose based on actual body weight, not the load.
7 milligrams per kilogram once daily
That is the tobramycin and gentamicin regimen.
1 gram regardless of weight
Vancomycin dosing in this lecture is weight-based.
25 to 30 milligrams per kilogram, rounded to the nearest 500 milligrams
Correct. The loading dose exists to reach the target trough quickly rather than waiting through several maintenance doses.

A.io: 5 — Antiviral classes
A.q: Which antiviral approach does the acyclovir family represent?
opts: Inhibiting viral assembly
Assembly inhibition is listed separately from nucleic acid synthesis.
Inhibiting nucleic acid synthesis
Correct — the drug is incorporated into viral DNA and terminates the chain.
Inhibiting viral release
That is oseltamivir's approach.
Blocking uncoating after entry
Uncoating blockade is a listed approach but not this family's.

A.io: 2 — Describe the molecular mechanism of action of dermatologic drugs
A.q: What is mupirocin's mechanism in the lecture?
opts: It interrupts the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane
That is polymyxin B.
It inhibits fungal ergosterol production and so prevents cell wall synthesis
That is the allylamines.
It binds bacterial transfer RNA, preventing protein synthesis
Correct, and the lecture notes it is not absorbed though it may irritate mucous membranes.
It prevents bacterial cell wall synthesis
That is bacitracin.

A.io: 9c — Azoles
A.q: Which azole penetrates the central nervous system and is therefore used in cryptococcal meningitis?
opts: Caspofungin
Caspofungin is an echinocandin, not an azole.
Fluconazole
Correct. It also has the best oral absorption of the group and is excreted in the urine, which suits it to candidiasis.
Ketoconazole
Ketoconazole explicitly does not enter the central nervous system.
Itraconazole
Itraconazole's indications are blastomycosis, histoplasmosis and onychomycosis.

A.io: 4k — Fluoroquinolones
A.q: What is the dual mechanism of action of the fluoroquinolones?
opts: Inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase, also called topoisomerase II, forming a quinolone-DNA-gyrase complex with induced DNA cleavage, plus inhibition of topoisomerase IV
Correct. The lecture notes the topoisomerase IV mechanism is poorly understood.
Inhibition of the 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits simultaneously
Fluoroquinolones do not act at the ribosome.
Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and blocks conversion of dihydrofolic acid to tetrahydrofolic acid; trimethoprim inhibits tetrahydropteroic acid synthetase upstream of it
That dual block is sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim.
Inhibition of cell wall cross-linking and of beta-lactamase
Neither applies to this class.

A.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
A.q: What are the two limits the lecture places on pralidoxime?
opts: It must be given orally, and it is inactivated by food
Route and food are not the stated limitations.
It reverses muscarinic but not nicotinic signs
The stated limits are central penetration and reversible inhibitors.
It does not enter the brain, and cannot overcome reversible inhibitors
Correct. It reactivates inhibited acetylcholinesterase but only within those limits.
It works only in children, and only within one hour of exposure
Neither limit is given in the lecture.

A.io: 3 — Classify the neurotransmitters released and the types of receptors found within the ANS
A.q: How does the lecture describe the nicotinic receptor?
opts: An intracellular receptor that binds acetylcholine after it crosses the membrane
The receptor sits in the membrane as a channel.
Five subunits forming a ligand-gated ion channel opened by two acetylcholine molecules
Correct, and it is found in the central nervous system, adrenal medulla, autonomic ganglia and neuromuscular junction.
A seven-transmembrane receptor coupled to a G protein and a second messenger
That is the muscarinic receptor family's arrangement rather than the nicotinic one.
An enzyme-linked receptor that phosphorylates intracellular targets on binding
The lecture describes an ion channel.

A.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
A.q: Which antisecretory use does the lecture give for atropine?
opts: Reducing bronchial secretions in asthma maintenance
The inhaled synthetic agents cover chronic obstructive pulmonary disease maintenance.
Preventing sweating in axillary hyperhidrosis
That is glycopyrronium.
Blocking respiratory tract secretions before surgery
Correct, and glycopyrrolate is used similarly before surgery.
Reducing gastric acid secretion in peptic ulcer disease
Not the use the lecture names.

A.io: 4n — Folate synthesis inhibitors
A.q: How do sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim block folate synthesis at two different steps?
opts: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits conversion of para-aminobenzoic acid to dihydrofolic acid via tetrahydropteroic acid synthetase; trimethoprim inhibits conversion of dihydrofolic acid to tetrahydrofolic acid via dihydrofolate reductase
Correct. Two sequential steps in one pathway, which is what makes the combination synergistic.

Sulfamethoxazole inhibits the conversion of dihydrofolic acid to tetrahydrofolic acid via dihydrofolate reductase; trimethoprim inhibits the conversion of para-aminobenzoic acid to dihydrofolic acid via tetrahydropteroic acid synthetase
This swaps the two enzymes.
Both inhibit dihydrofolate reductase, at different binding sites
They act at different steps of the pathway, not the same enzyme.
Sulfamethoxazole blocks folate absorption from the gut; trimethoprim blocks its renal reabsorption
Neither acts on absorption or reabsorption; both inhibit synthesis enzymes.

A.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
A.q: Which uses does the lecture list for propranolol beyond hypertension?
opts: Pheochromocytoma and clonidine withdrawal
Those are the alpha blockers.
Migraine, hyperthyroidism, angina and infarction
Correct, and after infarction it reduces infarct size and sudden death.
Glaucoma, asthma and benign prostatic hyperplasia
Glaucoma belongs to timolol; asthma is a contraindication.
Shock, cardiac arrest and anaphylaxis
Those are adrenergic agonist indications.

A.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
A.q: Which two problems does the lecture attach to intralesional steroid injection of an inflammatory nodule?
opts: Photosensitivity and severe sunburn
That belongs to the topical retinoids.
Systemic absorption leading to adrenal suppression, and local tissue atrophy
Correct. Both are consequences of injecting a steroid into the lesion.
Permanent hyperpigmentation and keloid formation
Neither is what the lecture lists for this route.
Bleaching of hair and clothing, together with staining of the surrounding skin at the injection site
That belongs to benzoyl peroxide.

A.io: 9c — Azoles
A.q: Itraconazole is useful in which infections?
opts: Zygomycete infection including Mucor and Rhizopus
Posaconazole is the azole named for the Zygomycetes.
Systemic aspergillosis as first-line therapy
Voriconazole took that role from amphotericin B.
Blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, onychomycosis, and febrile neutropenic patients not responding to antibiotics
Correct. It has an active metabolite and a wider spectrum than the ketoconazole it replaced.
Cryptococcal meningitis and prophylaxis against relapse in advanced acquired immunodeficiency syndrome
Those are fluconazole's indications, which follow from its central nervous system penetration.

A.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
A.q: Which adverse effect does the lecture attach to atracurium specifically?
opts: Malignant hyperthermia in susceptible people
That is succinylcholine with halothane.
Prolonged paralysis from pseudocholinesterase deficiency
That relates to succinylcholine's breakdown.
Rebound tachycardia on withdrawal
Not an effect described for this class.
Histamine release, with a fall in blood pressure and flushing
Correct, and it was replaced by its isomer cisatracurium for having fewer adverse effects.

A.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
A.q: What term does the lecture give as synonymous with an indirect-acting cholinergic agonist?
opts: Choline ester
Those are direct-acting agonists such as bethanechol and carbachol.
Anticholinesterase
Correct. They raise acetylcholine by blocking its degradation rather than binding the receptor.
Parasympatholytic
That is a cholinergic antagonist.
Antimuscarinic
That is also an antagonist term.

A.io: 9d — Allylamines
A.q: Which allylamine is available both orally and topically, and which is topical only?
opts: Naftifine is oral and topical; terbinafine is topical only
This reverses the two agents.
Both are available only topically
Terbinafine is orally active.
Both are available only orally
Naftifine is a topical agent.
Terbinafine is oral and topical; naftifine is topical only
Correct. Both inhibit squalene epoxidase and are used for superficial dermatophyte infection.

A.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
A.q: Which poisoning does the lecture say physostigmine treats?
opts: Overdose of anticholinergic drugs such as atropine
Correct. It raises acetylcholine to compete with the blocking drug.
Overdose of a cholinesterase inhibitor insecticide
That is treated with atropine and pralidoxime; giving another anticholinesterase would worsen it.
Beta blocker overdose
Not an indication given in this lecture.
Opioid overdose
Not an indication given in this lecture.

A.io: 8 — Anti-influenza agents
A.q: Why is influenza treatment framed around a season in this lecture?
opts: Flu season runs roughly October to March, which is when the illness is circulating
Correct, and it frames when an influenza-like illness should raise suspicion in the first place.
The drug is only manufactured and distributed during those particular months
Nothing about supply is described.
Resistance disappears outside the season
Resistance is described as an increasing problem over time, not a seasonal one.
Renal dosing requirements change with the season
Renal adjustment is not seasonal.

A.io: 5 — Antiviral classes
A.q: Several antivirals in this lecture are prodrugs. Which set is correct?
opts: Acyclovir, penciclovir, ganciclovir and zanamivir
Those are parent compounds rather than prodrugs.
Amphotericin B, caspofungin and griseofulvin
Those are antifungals, and none is described as a prodrug.
Metronidazole, linezolid and daptomycin
Those are antibacterials outside this objective.
Valacyclovir, famciclovir, valganciclovir and oseltamivir
Correct. Improving oral absorption is a recurring design theme across the whole antiviral section.

A.io: 6 — Anti-herpes agents
A.q: Why must renal function be watched during acyclovir therapy?
opts: The drug is nephrotoxic through direct tubular necrosis
Direct tubular damage is amphotericin B's mechanism.
Its vehicle accumulates in renal impairment
That is voriconazole's cyclodextrin.
It causes interstitial nephritis as a hypersensitivity reaction
Interstitial nephritis is listed among the aminopenicillin effects.
The drug crystallises in the renal tubule, so hydration must be maintained
Correct — a physical rather than a toxic mechanism of renal injury.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: Which uses does the lecture list for phenylephrine?
opts: Nasal decongestant, eye redness and septic shock
Correct.
Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
That is albuterol.
Hypertension and opiate withdrawal
That is clonidine.
Glaucoma
That is timolol or pilocarpine.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: Which vascular beds does dopamine dilate, and through which receptors?
opts: Renal and splanchnic, through dopaminergic receptors
Correct, which is distinct from its beta-one cardiac and high-dose alpha-one effects.
Coronary and cerebral, through beta-two receptors
Not the beds or receptors the lecture names.
Skeletal muscle beds, through alpha-two receptors
Alpha-two is presynaptic and central here.
Pulmonary vessels, through dopaminergic receptors
The lecture names renal and splanchnic arteries.

A.io: 10 — Outline appropriate patient education for dermatologic drugs
A.q: Which adverse effect of benzoyl peroxide most needs to be raised with a patient before they start it?
opts: It can bleach hair, clothing and bedding
Correct. This is the practical warning that prevents a patient ruining clothes and abandoning the drug.
It causes a permanent blue-grey discolouration of the skin
The lecture describes bleaching and irritation, not permanent pigmentation.
It commonly causes systemic hypersensitivity reactions
The lecture lists skin and mucous membrane irritation rather than systemic reactions.
It stains the skin orange for the duration of therapy
Bleaching rather than staining is what the lecture describes.

A.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
A.q: A patient develops pustular inflammation on the trunk a few weeks after starting a systemic corticosteroid. What does the lecture say happens when the steroid is stopped?
opts: Immediate and complete resolution of the eruption
The lecture specifically describes an initial worsening rather than clean resolution.
Conversion of the pustules into open comedones
This transformation is not described.
No change, because the eruption is independent of the drug
The eruption is drug induced, and the lecture ties its course to withdrawal.
An initial worsening, because inflammation increases
Correct, and warning the patient of this in advance is what stops them abandoning the plan.

A.io: 9c — Azoles
A.q: Which azole has the best oral absorption, and how is it eliminated?
opts: Posaconazole, excreted by the lungs
No such elimination route is described.
Fluconazole, excreted in the urine
Correct, and its urinary excretion is part of why a single dose treats vaginal candidiasis.
Ketoconazole, excreted in the bile
Ketoconazole must be taken with meals and is the most limited of the group.
Itraconazole, excreted unchanged in the faeces
Itraconazole is orally active with an active metabolite, but fluconazole is the one noted for best absorption.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: What does the lecture say distinguishes dobutamine from other sympathomimetics?
opts: It produces no tolerance with prolonged use
Tolerance may develop with prolonged use.
It barely raises myocardial oxygen demand
Correct, which matters in a failing heart.
It has no effect on atrioventricular conduction
It increases atrioventricular conduction, hence caution in atrial fibrillation.
It can be given orally
Route is not the distinguishing feature given.

A.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
A.q: Why is tyramine dangerous in a patient taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor?
opts: It blocks reuptake of norepinephrine at the terminal
That is cocaine's mechanism.
It is converted into amphetamine in the liver
No such conversion is described.
It directly stimulates alpha-one receptors
It acts indirectly, by displacing stored norepinephrine.
Monoamine oxidase normally destroys it in the gut
Correct, and it is found in fermented foods such as cheese and wine.

A.io: 4m — Polypeptides
A.q: What is the polymyxin mechanism of action?
opts: Binding the 30S ribosomal subunit and preventing transfer RNA from occupying the A site of the bacterial ribosome during chain elongation and protein assembly
That is the tetracycline mechanism.
Covalent inactivation of penicillin-binding proteins
That is the penicillin mechanism.
A detergent-like interaction with the lipopolysaccharide of the Gram-negative outer membrane, displacing magnesium and calcium and disrupting the membrane
Correct, which is why the spectrum is broad Gram-negative coverage — the target only exists there.
Inhibition of 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase in the cell wall
That is the echinocandin mechanism in fungi.

A.io: 4b — Cephalosporins
A.q: Cefazolin and cephalexin are first generation cephalosporins. What is their activity profile?
opts: Excellent Gram-positive activity with no Enterococcus coverage, and some Gram-negative coverage of Escherichia coli, Proteus and Klebsiella
Correct. The absence of Enterococcus coverage is a recurring theme across the whole cephalosporin class.
Excellent Gram-negative activity including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, with limited Gram-positive coverage and reliable activity against Enterococcus
That profile belongs to later generations and to specific antipseudomonal agents.
Broad coverage including anaerobes and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
Anaerobic and methicillin-resistant coverage are not features of the first generation.
Activity restricted to atypical organisms such as Legionella and Mycoplasma
Atypical coverage is a property of macrolides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.

A.io: 9e — Mitotic inhibitors
A.q: What should a patient be told about taking griseofulvin with food?
opts: It should be taken with an antacid to reduce gastric irritation
No such advice is given, and antacids interfere with other agents.
Absorption is increased by a high-fat meal, because the drug is very lipid soluble
Correct, and it is effective against numerous dermatophytes but not Candida, acting fungistatically.
It must be taken on an empty stomach, since food chelates and inactivates the drug
Chelation with food is the tetracycline and fluoroquinolone problem.
Food has no effect on absorption
A high-fat meal specifically increases absorption.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: Why does a local anaesthetic solution often contain epinephrine?
opts: It prevents an allergic reaction to the anaesthetic
Not the reason the lecture gives.
It causes vasoconstriction at the injection site
Correct, and applied topically it also helps control capillary oozing.
It speeds systemic absorption of the anaesthetic
Vasoconstriction slows removal from the site rather than speeding absorption.
It provides additional analgesia of its own
The benefit described is vascular, not analgesic.

A.io: 1 — Recall the gross organization of the nervous system, sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
A.q: How does the lecture divide the efferent division of the peripheral nervous system?
opts: Into the afferent system, carrying signals to the centre, and the enteric system, acting independently
Afferent is the other division of the peripheral nervous system entirely, not a branch of efferent.
Into the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems only, with no somatic component
Those two are subdivisions of the autonomic branch, and the somatic branch also exists.
Into the brain and the spinal cord, which together form the outflow
Brain and spinal cord are the central nervous system, not the efferent division.
Somatic, under voluntary control, and autonomic, under involuntary control
Correct. Afferent carries signals to the central nervous system; efferent carries them away and splits this way.

A.io: 2 — Describe the molecular mechanism of action of dermatologic drugs
A.q: What does imiquimod do, per the lecture?
opts: It corrects abnormal follicular keratinization, reduces bacterial counts within the follicle, and dampens the inflammatory response
That is a topical retinoid action.
It stimulates peripheral mononuclear cells to release interferon alpha and macrophages to produce tumour necrosis factor alpha and interleukins
Correct. It is an immunomodulator rather than a directly cytotoxic agent.
It inhibits T cell, mast cell and keratinocyte activation
That is tacrolimus and pimecrolimus, which suppress rather than stimulate.
It is converted to benzoic acid after crossing the stratum corneum
That is benzoyl peroxide.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: What does the lecture warn happens if oxymetazoline is used beyond three days?
opts: Permanent loss of the sense of smell
Not an effect the lecture describes.
Systemic hypertension requiring treatment
Rebound congestion is the stated risk.
Nasal septal perforation
Not described in this lecture.
Rhinitis medicamentosa, or rebound congestion
Correct, and it is the practical reason for a hard stop on a decongestant spray.

A.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
A.q: Which problem does the lecture specifically attach to topical neomycin?
opts: It causes hypopigmentation
That is azelaic acid.
It is inactivated by benzoyl peroxide
That interaction belongs to tretinoin.
It frequently causes sensitisation
Correct, and the class can also accumulate systemically.
It bleaches hair and clothing

The lecture matches the vehicle to the lesion rather than defaulting to the middle.

B.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
B.q: What does the lecture say happens with nicotine at autonomic ganglia?
opts: It permanently destroys ganglionic receptors
The effect is depolarizing blockade rather than destruction.
It depolarizes the ganglia, first stimulating and then paralysing them
Correct, and the stimulation raises blood pressure, heart rate, peristalsis and secretions before the fall.
It competitively and reversibly blocks them from the outset
All the ganglionic blockers except nicotine are nondepolarizing competitive antagonists.
It has no ganglionic action and acts only in the central nervous system
It is the exception among ganglionic agents in the lecture.

B.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
B.q: Why does the lecture prefer a selective beta-two agonist for chronic asthma over epinephrine?
opts: Greater potency at beta-two receptors
Duration, not potency, is the stated reason.
Oral availability
Albuterol is inhaled in this context.
Absence of any tremor
Tremor is in fact listed among albuterol's adverse effects.
Longer duration of action
Correct. Epinephrine reverses acute bronchospasm; albuterol covers chronic treatment.

B.io: 4h — Tetracyclines
B.q: Which tetracycline precautions relate to children and pregnancy?
opts: Cartilage damage — avoid under 18 years old
That caution belongs to the fluoroquinolones.
Kernicterus from bilirubin displacement — avoid in the first 30 days of life and throughout the third trimester of pregnancy
The neonatal restriction in this lecture attaches to ceftriaxone.
Grey baby syndrome — avoid in all trimesters
That is a chloramphenicol effect and is not the caution given here.
Discoloration of teeth and depression of skeletal growth — avoid under 8 years old and in the second and third trimesters
Correct. Both follow from the drug binding calcium in developing bone and teeth.

B.io: 1 — Categorizations of antimicrobial drugs
B.q: Under drug factors for choosing a regimen, which toxicities does the lecture list as the organ systems to consider?
opts: Hematologic, renal, hepatic, endocrine, vascular, lymphatic
Endocrine, vascular and lymphatic do not appear in the drug-factors framework.
Gastrointestinal, integument, hematologic, central nervous system, hepatic, renal
Correct. Six systems, and they map onto the monitoring parameters repeated for individual classes later in the lecture.
Cardiac, pulmonary, endocrine, musculoskeletal, ocular, and dermatologic systems
The lecture's list is different; cardiac effects appear later for specific agents rather than in this framework.
Gastrointestinal, renal, hepatic, ocular, reproductive, immunologic
Ocular, reproductive and immunologic are not part of the lecture's toxicity list at this point.

B.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
B.q: What is timolol's ocular action, and what is it used for?
opts: It reduces aqueous humour production
Correct, a different route to lowering pressure than pilocarpine's.
It causes miosis, for chronic open-angle glaucoma
Miosis is the cholinergic agonist route.
It causes mydriasis, for examination of the fundus
That is an antimuscarinic effect.
It reduces corneal oedema, for keratitis
Not an action described.

B.io: 4i — Aminoglycosides
B.q: Why did aminoglycoside dosing move from every 8 hours to every 24 hours?
opts: Once-daily dosing eliminates the need for therapeutic drug monitoring
Monitoring is still required; peaks and troughs are specified around the third or fourth dose.
Renal clearance is so rapid that more frequent dosing has no effect
Renal toxicity, not rapid clearance, is the dosing consideration named.
They show a post-antibiotic effect, so killing persists after the level falls, and concentration-dependent killing favours a large single dose
Correct. This is the clearest clinical application of the concentration-dependent pattern from earlier in the lecture.
They show time-dependent killing, so a longer interval keeps the level above the minimal inhibitory concentration for a greater share of the dosing period
Time-dependent killing argues for frequent or continuous dosing, which is the opposite.

B.io: 8 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic antagonists
B.q: What do ganglionic blockers do, and why are they rarely used?
opts: They block alpha and beta receptors simultaneously
That describes labetalol and carvedilol among the adrenergic antagonists.
They block nicotinic receptors at sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia
Correct, and blocking everything at once is precisely why they are rarely used clinically.
They block muscarinic receptors only, sparing the sympathetic system
That is the antimuscarinic group.
They act at the neuromuscular junction to relax skeletal muscle
That is the neuromuscular blocking agents.

B.io: 9b — Polyenes
B.q: Which polyene is used specifically for oral candidiasis?
opts: Natamycin
Natamycin is named among the polyenes but the oral candidiasis agent specified is nystatin.
Caspofungin
Caspofungin is an echinocandin used for oesophageal candidiasis intravenously.
Nystatin
Correct, available as oral preparations and a topical powder, with systemic effects limited by poor absorption.
Amphotericin B deoxycholate
That is the systemic intravenous agent.

B.io: 6 — Anti-herpes agents
B.q: Which central nervous system effects are listed for acyclovir?
opts: Confusion, ataxia, seizures and coma
That fuller list belongs to ganciclovir and valganciclovir.
Peripheral neuropathy and tendon rupture
Those are fluoroquinolone effects.
Visual disturbance in about 30 percent of patients
That is voriconazole.
Seizures, delirium and tremor
Correct, alongside nausea, vomiting, rash and bone marrow suppression.

B.io: 7 — Identify contraindications for dermatologic drugs
B.q: Which patient should not be given a topical retinoid, per the lecture?
opts: A patient over sixty years of age
Age is not a contraindication, and the lecture notes retinoids are useful for wrinkles and dyspigmentation.
A patient who is pregnant
Correct. The lecture says to avoid retinoids during pregnancy.
A patient with a history of eczema
Eczema is not given as a contraindication to topical retinoid therapy.
A patient taking an oral contraceptive
Oral contraceptives are listed as a useful acne therapy in some women, not a conflict.

B.io: 5 — Antiviral classes
B.q: A patient presents on day 4 of an influenza-like illness. What does the lecture imply about oseltamivir?
opts: Treatment is equally effective at any point in the illness
The lecture is explicit that it must be started as soon as possible.
Acyclovir should be substituted
Acyclovir has no activity against influenza.
The 48-hour window for starting treatment has passed
Correct. Because the drug blocks release of new virus rather than clearing existing virus, starting late has little to act on.
Treatment should be started at a doubled dose to compensate
No dose escalation strategy is described, and dosing is not tested.

B.io: 4m — Polypeptides
B.q: What are the black box warnings for the polymyxins?
opts: Ototoxicity, red man syndrome, and phlebitis
Those are vancomycin concerns.
Nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade
Correct. These are the only warnings the lecture labels explicitly as black box, which is why they are worth holding separately from ordinary adverse effects.
Tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and central nervous system effects
Those are fluoroquinolone adverse effects and are not labelled black box in this deck.
Thrombocytopenia, serotonin syndrome, and hypertensive crisis
Those are linezolid concerns.

B.io: 9 — Antifungal classes
B.q: A patient develops athlete's foot after prolonged use of occlusive footwear. Which predisposing factor is this?
opts: Loss of barriers
That covers burns, surgery and catheters breaching a physical boundary.
Immunodeficiency
That covers cancer, human immunodeficiency virus infection, transplant and chemotherapy.
Metabolic abnormality
That category is illustrated by diabetes.
A warm moist environment
Correct — the lecture's own examples for that category are diaper rash and athlete's foot.

B.io: 2 — Common modes of action of antimicrobial agents
B.q: Which antibiotic classes bind the 50S ribosomal subunit, and which bind the 30S?
opts: 50S — vancomycin, daptomycin; 30S — linezolid, tigecycline
Vancomycin and daptomycin act at the cell wall and membrane rather than the ribosome.
50S — macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, streptogramins; 30S — aminoglycosides, tetracyclines
Correct. The bacterial ribosome is 70S against the mammalian 80S, which is the basis for selectivity.
50S — aminoglycosides, tetracyclines; 30S — macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, streptogramins
This reverses the two groups.
50S — fluoroquinolones, metronidazole; 30S — penicillins, cephalosporins
None of those four is a protein synthesis inhibitor; they act on DNA or the cell wall.

B.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
B.q: Which uses does the lecture list for neostigmine?
opts: Slowing the progression of Alzheimer disease
That is the donepezil group.
Treating an overdose of an anticholinergic drug
That is physostigmine, which enters the central nervous system.
Stimulating the bladder and gut, and reversing competitive blockade
Correct, and it can stimulate contractility before paralysing.
Diagnosing myasthenia gravis and assessing cholinesterase therapy
Those are edrophonium's roles.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: A genetically susceptible patient given succinylcholine with halothane develops muscular rigidity, metabolic acidosis, tachycardia and a very high temperature. What does the lecture direct?
opts: Pralidoxime to reactivate acetylcholinesterase
That is for anticholinesterase poisoning.
Atropine to oppose muscarinic overactivity
This is not a cholinergic crisis.
Neostigmine to reverse the blockade
Reversal is irrelevant to the hyperthermic reaction.
Rapid cooling and dantrolene
Correct, and blocking that release is what reduces heat production.

C.io: 6 — Summarize the synthesis, release, and subsequent destiny of ANS neurotransmitters
C.q: How does guanethidine act?
opts: It blocks transport of transmitters into storage vesicles
That is reserpine.
It blocks postsynaptic alpha-one receptors
That is the prazosin group.
It stimulates presynaptic alpha-two receptors
That is clonidine.
It blocks release of stored norepinephrine
Correct, which is distinct from reserpine's blockade of vesicular uptake.

C.io: 1 — Identify dermatologic drug classes and commonly prescribed dermatologic drugs
C.q: Which set gives the MAJOR indicators of atopic dermatitis as the lecture lists them?
opts: Raised immunoglobulin E, positive allergy skin tests, and dry patchy scales
These are listed as minor indicators rather than major ones.
Nikolsky sign, mucosal erosion at two or more sites, and fever preceding the rash by one to three days
None of these belong to the lecture's atopic dermatitis criteria.
Comedones, papulopustular lesions, and nodules
These are acne lesions.
Pruritus, rash in areas typical of the disease, chronic or repeated symptoms, and family history
Correct. Raised immunoglobulin E, positive skin tests, dry patchy scales and infection susceptibility are the minor ones.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: Through which receptor does amphetamine raise blood pressure?
opts: Beta-two
Beta-two would dilate rather than constrict.
Alpha-two
Alpha-two reduces sympathetic outflow.
Dopaminergic
Not the vascular route described.
Alpha-one
Correct, with beta-one accounting for the cardiac stimulation.

C.io: 4b — Cephalosporins
C.q: Which cephalosporin provides methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus coverage?
opts: Ceftriaxone, a third generation agent
Ceftriaxone has good Streptococcus coverage but no methicillin-resistant activity.
Ceftaroline, a fifth generation agent
Correct. It is the cephalosporin that breaks the class's usual absence of methicillin-resistant coverage, and it must be renally adjusted.
Cefepime, a fourth generation agent
Cefepime explicitly lacks methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus coverage.
Ceftolozane/tazobactam, a fifth generation agent
This fifth generation combination also lacks methicillin-resistant coverage; its strength is antipseudomonal activity.

C.io: 1 — Recall the gross organization of the nervous system, sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
C.q: Which three systems make up the autonomic division in the lecture?
opts: Afferent, efferent and enteric
Afferent and efferent are the two divisions of the peripheral nervous system as a whole.
Central, peripheral and enteric
Central and peripheral are the two anatomical divisions of the nervous system overall.
Enteric, parasympathetic and sympathetic
Correct. The enteric system is the one most often forgotten of the three.
Somatic, parasympathetic and sympathetic
The somatic system is the other efferent branch, not part of the autonomic division.

C.io: 4b — Cephalosporins
C.q: What distinguishes ceftriaxone from most other cephalosporins in renal impairment?
opts: It must be dialysed off before each subsequent dose
Nothing in the lecture supports this.
It requires no dosage adjustment in renal insufficiency
Correct, and it is a useful contrast because the class as a whole is mostly renally eliminated.
It requires the largest dose reduction of any cephalosporin in renal insufficiency
The opposite is stated — no adjustment is needed.
It is contraindicated at any degree of renal impairment
No such contraindication is given; the caution attached to ceftriaxone concerns the first 30 days of life.

C.io: 4k — Fluoroquinolones
C.q: What collateral consequence of fluoroquinolone overuse does the lecture emphasise?
opts: Permanent loss of Gram-positive coverage across the entire class
Resistance is described in general terms, not as a loss of Gram-positive activity specifically.
Cross-resistance to all beta-lactams
No such cross-resistance is claimed.
High rates of resistance, and Clostridium difficile as collateral damage
Correct. The slide states overuse equals resistance in capital letters, which is a deliberate emphasis.
Accelerated hepatic metabolism of co-administered drugs
Fluoroquinolones inhibit CYP1A2 rather than inducing metabolism.

C.io: 7 — Anti-cytomegalovirus agents
C.q: What proportion of patients must stop intravenous ganciclovir because of side effects?
opts: About 1 in 20
The lecture gives a far higher proportion.
Almost none; it is generally well tolerated
It is poorly tolerated, which is the point of the slide.
Essentially all patients
The figure given is around a third rather than universal.
About a third
Correct — a striking figure, and the reason the better-absorbed oral prodrug matters clinically.

C.io: 9 — Antifungal classes
C.q: Which organisms cause the superficial mycoses of hair, nails and mucous membranes?
opts: Chromomycosis, Pseudallescheriasis and Sporotrichosis
Those are subcutaneous, affecting the skin layers rather than hair and nails.
Candida, Coccidioides and Blastomyces
Those appear in the systemic group.
Epidermophyton, Microsporum and Trichophyton
Correct. These are the dermatophytes that griseofulvin and the allylamines treat.
Aspergillus, Cryptococcus and Histoplasma
Those cause systemic mycoses of internal organs.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: Which vascular effect does propranolol produce, and through which receptor?
opts: Renal vasodilation, through dopaminergic receptors
That is dopamine.
Peripheral vasoconstriction, through beta-two blockade
Correct, since blocking beta-two removes vasodilation.
Peripheral vasodilation, through alpha-one blockade
Propranolol does not affect alpha receptors.
No vascular effect at all
Vasoconstriction is listed among its actions.

C.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
C.q: Why does the lecture say an azole is sometimes combined with a corticosteroid?
opts: To prevent the development of resistance
Resistance is raised for erythromycin in acne, not as the reason for this combination.
To allow a shorter total course of therapy
The lecture still describes treatment as generally prolonged.
To make the preparation less irritating to the skin
Local irritation is listed as the adverse reaction, but symptom relief is the stated reason.
For more rapid symptom relief
Correct. The steroid addresses symptoms while the antifungal addresses the organism.

C.io: 10 — Outline appropriate patient education for dermatologic drugs
C.q: What does the lecture advise patients about washing in acne?
opts: Wash with a high pH soap several times daily, since a raised pH increases the activity of other topical agents
A high pH may degrade the activity of other agents and is less tolerable on the skin.
Avoid washing the affected area entirely while on treatment
Cleansing is part of non-pharmacologic therapy rather than something to avoid.
Do not wash too frequently; twice a day, balancing cleanliness against drying and irritation
Correct, and it adds that once rinsed off no active product remains on the skin.
Wash as often as possible to remove surface oils
Excessive scrubbing and washing is listed as a contributory factor, so this would worsen the disease.

C.io: 6 — Summarize the synthesis, release, and subsequent destiny of ANS neurotransmitters
C.q: Which sequence describes neurotransmission at a cholinergic neuron in the lecture?
opts: Synthesis, storage, release, and inactivation by catechol-O-methyltransferase
That enzyme inactivates catecholamines, not acetylcholine.
Storage, release, binding, and permanent removal of choline from the neuron
Choline is recycled rather than lost.
Synthesis, storage, release, receptor binding, degradation, recycling of choline
Correct. Six sequential steps, and several drug classes act at one of them.
Synthesis, release, reuptake into the presynaptic terminal, and repackaging without degradation
Reuptake of the intact transmitter is the adrenergic pattern; acetylcholine is degraded in the cleft.

C.io: 9c — Azoles
C.q: Why does voriconazole's intravenous formulation require caution in renal failure?
opts: Its vehicle, cyclodextrin, accumulates when renal function is impaired
Correct — the concern is the vehicle rather than the drug itself, which is an unusual reason to avoid a formulation.
The drug itself is cleared entirely by glomerular filtration and reaches toxic levels
The stated problem is accumulation of the vehicle.
It crystallises in the renal tubule as acyclovir does
Tubular crystallisation is an acyclovir effect.
It causes direct renal tubule damage requiring saline hydration
That is amphotericin B's toxicity.

C.io: 7 — Identify contraindications for dermatologic drugs
C.q: Which patient does the lecture say should avoid topical tacrolimus or pimecrolimus?
opts: A patient using an emollient
Emollients are part of routine care and are not a conflict.
A patient with a weakened immune system
Correct, and the lecture pairs this with a possible cancer risk.
A patient with a history of acne
Acne is not a stated contraindication for these agents.
A patient over the age of sixty
Age alone is not given as a bar.

C.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
C.q: How is norepinephrine given, per the lecture?
opts: As a single intramuscular injection
That route is listed for epinephrine.
Orally, in divided doses
Catecholamines are not effective orally.
By inhalation
Inhalation is listed for epinephrine, not norepinephrine.
As a titrated intravenous infusion
Correct, which suits a drug used to support vascular resistance in shock.

C.io: 8 — Anti-influenza agents
C.q: What kind of compound is oseltamivir as administered?
opts: A prodrug converted to its carboxylate form
Correct — another prodrug in a lecture full of them, alongside valacyclovir, famciclovir and valganciclovir.
An active guanine analogue requiring no conversion
It requires conversion, and it is not a guanine analogue.
A monoclonal antibody against viral haemagglutinin
No antibody therapy is described here.
A live attenuated preparation
That would describe a vaccine rather than an antiviral drug.

C.io: 9 — Antifungal classes
C.q: A patient develops oral candidiasis after a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which predisposing factor does this illustrate?
opts: Suppression of competing organisms
Correct. Removing the bacterial flora leaves the niche open, which is why antibiotic exposure is itself a fungal risk factor.
Loss of barriers
Loss of barriers refers to burns, surgery and catheters breaching a physical boundary.
Metabolic abnormality
That category is illustrated by diabetes rather than by antibiotic exposure.
A warm and moist local environment
That category covers diaper rash and athlete's foot.

C.io: 7 — Identify contraindications for dermatologic drugs
C.q: What does the lecture say about isotretinoin and pregnancy?
opts: It is contraindicated only in the first trimester
The lecture gives no trimester-limited allowance.
It requires no pregnancy precautions because it is applied topically
Isotretinoin here is the systemic retinoid, not a topical agent.
It is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and the lecture adds that men should avoid it as well
Correct, and the iPledge programme exists around exactly this risk.
It is safe in the second and third trimesters, and only the first trimester requires contraceptive cover
It is contraindicated, without a safe window.

C.io: 7 — Anti-cytomegalovirus agents
C.q: Which central nervous system effects are listed for ganciclovir?
opts: Blurred vision and mental confusion from enzyme induction
That profile belongs to griseofulvin.
Confusion, ataxia, seizures and coma
Correct, occurring in a minority of patients alongside the haematologic effects.
Seizures, delirium and tremor only
That shorter list is acyclovir's.
Peripheral neuropathy and tendon injury
Those are fluoroquinolone effects.

C.io: 10 — Outline appropriate patient education for dermatologic drugs
C.q: A patient asks about the ciclopirox nail lacquer for onychomycosis. What does the lecture say about how well it works?
opts: It works only on fingernails, not toenails
The lecture markets it for both fingernails and toenails.
It is as effective as oral terbinafine
No such comparison is made, and the stated efficacy is low.
It is less than twelve per cent effective
Correct, and saying so up front is what keeps expectations honest for a months-long treatment.
It is curative in the majority of patients
The lecture reports a low success rate, not a majority.

C.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
C.q: Which of the two does the lecture link to preventing cardiovascular mortality in heart failure?
opts: Carvedilol
Correct, and it also decreases lipid peroxidation and vascular wall thickening.
Labetalol
Labetalol is the one given intravenously for hypertensive emergencies.
Propranolol
Propranolol's post-infarction benefit is described separately.
Pindolol
Pindolol is noted for intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.

C.io: 6 — Summarize the synthesis, release, and subsequent destiny of ANS neurotransmitters
C.q: How do the indirect-acting cholinergic agents work?
opts: They block reuptake of acetylcholine into the presynaptic terminal
Acetylcholine is degraded in the cleft rather than taken back up intact.
They increase the activity of acetylcholine by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase
Correct. They raise the transmitter rather than binding the receptor themselves.
They bind muscarinic receptors directly and mimic acetylcholine
That is the direct-acting group.
They increase synthesis of acetylcholine from acetyl coenzyme A and choline
The lecture attributes their effect to blocking degradation, not to increasing synthesis.

C.io: 5 — Antiviral classes
C.q: Which of the listed antiviral approaches works on the host rather than on the virus?
opts: Inhibiting viral protein synthesis
That acts on the virus.
Stimulating the host immune system
Correct — it is the only one of the eight aimed at the host side of the interaction.
Inhibiting specific viral enzymes
That acts on the virus.
Blocking viral assembly
That acts on the virus.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: What does the lecture say nicotine does at the nicotinic receptor across concentrations?
opts: It has no effect on the nicotinic receptor, acting only at muscarinic sites
The receptor is named for nicotine's action on it.
It stimulates the receptor at low concentrations and blocks it at high concentrations
Correct, which is why nicotine appears in both the agonist and the ganglionic blocker discussions.
It stimulates the receptor at all concentrations, increasing with dose
The relationship reverses at high concentration.
It blocks the receptor at all concentrations
At low concentration it stimulates.

C.io: 4o — Nitroimidazoles
C.q: What is metronidazole's mechanism of action?
opts: It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
That is trimethoprim.
It interacts with bacterial DNA to cause loss of helical structure and strand breakage
Correct, and its activity spans Gram-positive and Gram-negative anaerobes plus parasites.
It inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
That is the fluoroquinolone mechanism.
It binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks the transpeptidation step of protein synthesis
That is the macrolide mechanism.

C.io: 1 — Recall the gross organization of the nervous system, sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
C.q: What does the afferent division of the peripheral nervous system do, and what example does the lecture give?
opts: It connects preganglionic to postganglionic neurons within a ganglion
That describes the efferent relay rather than the afferent division.
It controls gastrointestinal motility independently of the brain
That is the enteric system.
It carries signals to the central nervous system
Correct. The reflex arc needs the incoming limb before any autonomic outflow can be adjusted.
It carries signals away from the central nervous system to skeletal muscle
Carrying signals away is the efferent division.

C.io: 6 — Summarize the synthesis, release, and subsequent destiny of ANS neurotransmitters
C.q: How does reserpine act?
opts: It blocks transmitter uptake into vesicles
Correct, depleting norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin.
It blocks release of stored norepinephrine from vesicles
That is guanethidine.
It blocks reuptake of norepinephrine at the terminal
That is cocaine.
It inhibits monoamine oxidase within the neuron
Reserpine works on vesicular transport, not the enzyme.

C.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
C.q: What is intravenous labetalol used for?
opts: Hypertensive emergencies
Correct, using its combined alpha and beta blockade.
Chronic open-angle glaucoma
That is timolol.
Acute asthma
A beta blocker would worsen bronchospasm.
Septic shock
That is an adrenergic agonist indication.

C.io: 4m — Polypeptides
C.q: Why is polymyxin resistance uncommon, and why is use expected to increase?
opts: The class went largely unused for the last 50 years, and rising multidrug resistance is bringing it back despite optimal regimens not being well studied
Correct. Low historical exposure is the reason resistance never developed widely.
The mechanism is impossible for bacteria to circumvent, and newer formulations have removed the nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity entirely
Proposed resistance mechanisms are listed, and the black box toxicities remain.
It is used only topically, so systemic resistance cannot emerge
Route is not the explanation offered.
It is always combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor that prevents resistance
No such combination is described.

C.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
C.q: Besides blocking norepinephrine reuptake, what other action does the lecture give cocaine?
opts: It inhibits monoamine oxidase
Not an action described for cocaine here.
It depletes vesicular stores of norepinephrine
That is reserpine and guanethidine.
It stimulates dopaminergic receptors in the kidney
That is dopamine's renal effect.
It blocks neuronal sodium channels
Correct, and it also blocks sodium-potassium activated ATPase.

C.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
C.q: Which agents does the lecture call the gold standard for atopic dermatitis?
opts: Oral corticosteroids
These are used for short courses during exacerbations rather than as the standard.
Sedating antihistamines
These address night-time itching rather than the disease itself.
Topical corticosteroids
Correct, with the agent chosen by severity and by site of disease.
Topical immunomodulators
Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus are named as second line, after topical steroids.

C.io: 9c — Azoles
C.q: Which azoles are noted as teratogenic?
opts: None of the azoles carries a teratogenicity caution
Several do.
Only the topical imidazole derivatives
The topical agents are listed without that caution; the systemic ones carry it.
Itraconazole, and fluconazole and voriconazole in animals
Correct. Reproductive safety is a recurring caution across the azole group.
Ketoconazole and posaconazole only
Teratogenicity is attributed to itraconazole, fluconazole and voriconazole in this deck.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: What are atropine's effects on the eye?
opts: No ocular effect at any dose
Ophthalmic dilation is one of its listed therapeutic uses.
Persistent mydriasis and cycloplegia
Correct, which is the opposite of the miosis and accommodation spasm the agonists cause.
Miosis with spasm of accommodation
That is the cholinergic agonist picture, carbachol and pilocarpine.
Reduced aqueous humour production with no change in pupil size
That is timolol.

C.io: 2 — Common modes of action of antimicrobial agents
C.q: Which features of fungal cells explain why antibacterial antibiotics do not treat them?
opts: They replicate only inside host cells, so extracellular antibiotics never reach them
Obligate intracellular replication describes viruses, not fungi.
They are eukaryotic, with a rigid cell wall containing chitin, a cell membrane built on ergosterol, different ribosomes and a distinct nuclear membrane
Correct. Every antifungal class in this lecture exploits one of these differences, which is also why selectivity is harder than with bacteria.
They are prokaryotic, with a peptidoglycan cell wall and a 70S ribosome that antibacterial agents cannot reach, and a nuclear region without a surrounding membrane
Fungi are eukaryotic; peptidoglycan and the 70S ribosome are bacterial features.
They lack a cell wall entirely and rely on a cholesterol membrane, so cell wall agents have no target
Fungi do have a cell wall, of chitin, and the membrane sterol is ergosterol rather than cholesterol.

C.io: 8 — Anti-influenza agents
C.q: What happens to newly formed influenza virions when neuraminidase is inhibited?
opts: Their nucleic acid cannot be replicated
Nucleic acid inhibition is the guanine analogues' approach.
They cannot be cleaved free of the host cell as budding progeny
Correct — they remain tethered at the surface, so the infection cannot spread to new cells.
They can no longer attach to the receptor on the next host cell
Attachment is a separate step, and blocking it is a different listed approach.
They cannot uncoat once inside the next cell
Uncoating is another distinct approach in the list.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: Which additional effect does carbachol produce through its nicotinic action?
opts: Release of epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
Correct, which is why its cardiovascular and gastrointestinal effects can be profound and biphasic.
Direct blockade of the neuromuscular junction
That is the neuromuscular blocking agents.
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase
Carbachol binds the receptor directly rather than blocking the enzyme.
Depletion of stored norepinephrine
That is reserpine and guanethidine.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: A patient is agitated and hallucinating, with dilated pupils, flushed dry skin, fever, urinary retention and a fast heart. Which toxidrome is this?
opts: Nicotinic, from ganglionic stimulation
That gives fasciculations and weakness with hypertension.
Beta blocker overdose
That would give bradycardia and bronchoconstriction rather than this picture.
Anticholinergic
Correct. The lecture gives it as mad as a hatter, blind as a bat, red as a beet, dry as a bone, hot as Hades, with retention and tachycardia.
Muscarinic, from a cholinergic agonist
That runs wet and slow: salivation, lacrimation, miosis and bradycardia.

C.io: 5 — Identify the location and effects of alpha-one, alpha-two, beta-one and beta-two stimulation
C.q: Where are adrenergic receptors located relative to the synapse?
opts: Only postsynaptically on the effector organ
Alpha-two receptors sit presynaptically.
Only presynaptically on the neuron
Alpha-one and the beta receptors act postsynaptically.
Only within the central nervous system
They are found peripherally as well.
Presynaptically or postsynaptically
Correct, and that presynaptic location is what alpha-two agonists exploit.

C.io: 4n — Folate synthesis inhibitors
C.q: Which drug interaction of sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim involves cytochrome P450 2C9 inhibition?
opts: Reduced effectiveness of oral contraceptives through gut flora disruption
That is the aminopenicillin interaction.
Serotonin syndrome with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
That is linezolid.
Chelation reducing absorption of iron supplements
Chelation belongs to tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
A significant increase in the international normalised ratio in patients on warfarin
Correct. Other interactions include raised phenytoin, rifampin and digoxin levels, reduced methotrexate clearance, and hypoglycaemia with sulfonylureas.

C.io: 4i — Aminoglycosides
C.q: Which toxicities define the aminoglycoside class?
opts: Renal toxicity and ototoxicity, requiring renal dose adjustment
Correct, and vancomycin shares both, which is why the combination is watched carefully.
Hepatotoxicity and thrombocytopenia
Thrombocytopenia is the linezolid concern; hepatic effects belong to other agents.
Tendon rupture and peripheral neuropathy
Those are fluoroquinolone effects.
Serotonin syndrome, hypertensive crisis, and thrombocytopenia
Those follow from linezolid's interactions.

C.io: 4i — Aminoglycosides
C.q: Aminoglycosides are the drug of choice for which situations?
opts: Clostridium difficile colitis
That is treated with metronidazole or oral vancomycin.
Febrile neutropenia, sepsis, and enterococcal synergy
Correct, with Enterococcus covered only at synergy dosing rather than as monotherapy.
Community-acquired pneumonia and acute otitis media
Those are macrolide, aminopenicillin and respiratory fluoroquinolone indications.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus skin infection
Aminoglycoside activity is against Gram-negatives, not resistant Gram-positives.

C.io: 9b — Polyenes
C.q: Why are fever and chills expected during an amphotericin B infusion, and how are they managed?
opts: They are caused by rapid fungal lysis releasing endotoxin into the circulation, and are prevented by slowing the rate of the infusion alone
Endotoxin release is not the mechanism described, and premedication is the stated management.
They are a disulfiram-like reaction to the infusion vehicle, and are avoided by withholding alcohol
The disulfiram-like reaction belongs to metronidazole.
They are driven by interleukin-1 and tumour necrosis factor, and patients are pretreated with acetaminophen, antihistamines and corticosteroids
Correct. The reaction is a cytokine response rather than an allergy, which is why premedication works.
They reflect an immunoglobulin E mediated allergic reaction, and the drug must be stopped permanently
The mechanism given is cytokine-mediated, and the reaction is managed by premedication rather than by discontinuation.

C.io: 4b — Cephalosporins
C.q: What is the approximate rate of penicillin cross-sensitivity with cephalosporins in this lecture?
opts: Approximately 10 percent
Ten percent is a commonly repeated older figure, but the lecture gives a much lower one.
Approximately 25 percent
That would make cephalosporins largely unusable after a penicillin reaction, which is not the case.
Cross-sensitivity does not occur at all between the two classes
The lecture states cross-sensitivity exists, just at a low rate.
Less than 1 percent
Correct. The figure matters clinically because a reported penicillin allergy does not automatically exclude a cephalosporin.

C.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
C.q: Which use does the lecture give for mupirocin beyond ordinary skin infection?
opts: Treating onychomycosis of the toenails
That is the ciclopirox nail lacquer.
Eliminating nasal carriage of Staphylococcus aureus
Correct, and its coverage is most gram positive aerobes, especially meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
Eliminating vulvovaginal candidiasis in women
That indication belongs to the azole antifungals.
Treating recurrent orolabial herpes simplex
That is acyclovir and penciclovir.

C.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
C.q: What does the lecture say about cardioselectivity at higher doses?
opts: It increases
The lecture states the opposite.
It is unchanged
Selectivity is dose dependent.
It converts to alpha blockade
No such conversion occurs.
It is lost
Correct, so a beta-one selective agent can still affect the airway.

C.io: 4 — Describe absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of dermatologic drugs
C.q: A patient's corticosteroid is not controlling a plaque. Based on the concentration gradient principle in the lecture, what does that principle predict?
opts: Raising the concentration increases drug transfer and can overcome the resistance
Correct. The lecture gives corticosteroid resistance overcome by increased concentration as its worked example.
Concentration has little effect once the stratum corneum is saturated
The lecture states the opposite: increased concentration means increased drug transfer.
Changing to a more drying vehicle will matter more than concentration
Vehicle is a separate variable in the lecture; the concentration gradient is its own principle.
Only a change to a systemic agent will overcome it
Systemic therapy is reserved for moderate-severe disease, not for a single unresponsive plaque.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: Why does the lecture suggest a small dose of a nondepolarizing blocker before succinylcholine?
opts: To prolong the duration of the block
That is not the stated purpose.
To prevent malignant hyperthermia
That risk is managed by avoiding the trigger and treating with dantrolene.
To allow a lower dose of anaesthetic agent
Reduced anaesthetic requirement is attributed to neuromuscular blockade generally.
To prevent the fasciculations that cause muscle soreness
Correct. It is a comfort measure that addresses a predictable adverse effect.

C.io: 4a — Penicillins
C.q: Which penicillin dosage form is given intramuscularly as a single long-acting dose?
opts: Penicillin V potassium (Pen VK)
Penicillin V potassium is the oral form, chosen because it is stable in stomach acid.
Penicillin G (benzylpenicillin)
Plain penicillin G is the intravenous form, dosed 18 to 24 million units daily in divided doses.
Ampicillin sodium
Ampicillin is an aminopenicillin given intravenously or orally, not a long-acting intramuscular depot.
Penicillin G benzathine (Bicillin)
Correct. The benzathine salt is the depot form, which is why one injection can cover an indication such as syphilis.

C.io: 9a — Echinocandins
C.q: Which adverse reactions are listed for the echinocandins?
opts: Visual disturbance and hepatic dysfunction
Those belong to voriconazole.
Bone marrow suppression and hepatotoxicity as the principal dose-limiting effects
Those are flucytosine's effects.
Renal tubule damage requiring saline hydration
That is amphotericin B.
Tachycardia, headache, insomnia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and blood dyscrasias
Correct. Note the electrolyte disturbances overlap with amphotericin B's, despite a completely different mechanism.

C.io: 8 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic antagonists
C.q: Which three classes make up the cholinergic antagonists in the lecture?
opts: Antimuscarinic agents, ganglionic blockers and neuromuscular blocking agents
Correct, and they are distinguished by which cholinergic site they occupy.
Direct-acting agents, indirect-acting agents and reactivators
That framework belongs to the cholinergic agonists.
Alpha blockers, beta blockers and mixed blockers
Those are adrenergic antagonists.
Choline esters, alkaloids and anticholinesterases
Those are all agonist groups.

C.io: 7 — Anti-cytomegalovirus agents
C.q: Which of ganciclovir and valganciclovir is the better-absorbed oral form?
opts: Both are equally absorbed
The prodrug is substantially better absorbed.
Neither is absorbed orally; both are intravenous only
Valganciclovir is an oral agent.
Valganciclovir, the prodrug
Correct. Ganciclovir's oral bioavailability is very low, which is why the prodrug exists.
Ganciclovir, the parent compound
Ganciclovir is the poorly absorbed parent.

C.io: 9c — Azoles
C.q: Voriconazole is derived from which other azole?
opts: Ketoconazole
Ketoconazole is the oldest of the group and is not voriconazole's parent.
Clotrimazole
Clotrimazole is a topical imidazole derivative.
Fluconazole
Correct — a fluconazole derivative introduced in 2002, which then took over systemic aspergillosis from amphotericin B.
Itraconazole
Posaconazole, not voriconazole, is the agent related to itraconazole.

C.io: 5 — Identify the location and effects of alpha-one, alpha-two, beta-one and beta-two stimulation
C.q: Which receptors does oxymetazoline act on?
opts: Alpha-one and alpha-two
Correct, producing vasoconstriction.
Beta-one and beta-two
Those are isoproterenol's.
Alpha-one only
Phenylephrine is the selective alpha-one agent.
Dopaminergic
Those are dopamine's renal targets.

C.io: 9b — Polyenes
C.q: Which three polyene agents does the lecture name?
opts: Ketoconazole, miconazole and clotrimazole
Those are imidazoles.
Griseofulvin, terbinafine and naftifine
Griseofulvin is a mitotic inhibitor and the other two are allylamines.
Amphotericin B, nystatin and natamycin
Correct. Amphotericin B is the systemic agent; nystatin is used topically and orally because it is poorly absorbed.
Caspofungin, micafungin and anidulafungin
Those are echinocandins.

C.io: 4j — Glycopeptides & lipopeptides
C.q: Which infusion-related reaction is characteristic of vancomycin?
opts: Tendonitis and Achilles tendon rupture
That belongs to the fluoroquinolones.
Red man syndrome, along with fever, chills and phlebitis
Correct, and it sits alongside ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity among the monitoring concerns.
Disulfiram-like reaction when combined with ethanol
That is the metronidazole reaction.
Serotonin syndrome when combined with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
That is the linezolid interaction.

C.io: 5 — Antiviral classes
C.q: Which antiviral approach does oseltamivir represent?
opts: Inhibiting viral release
Correct — neuraminidase frees budding progeny, so blocking it traps new virus at the cell surface.
Blocking viral attachment to cells
Attachment blockade is a listed approach but not this drug's.
Inhibiting nucleic acid synthesis
That is the acyclovir family's approach.
Stimulating the host immune system
That approach is listed but is not oseltamivir's mechanism.

C.io: 9 — Antifungal classes
C.q: With which agents is flucytosine combined, and for what?
opts: With amphotericin B in cryptococcal meningitis, and with itraconazole in chromoblastomycosis
Correct. It is used in combination rather than alone, and its own indications are Cryptococcus neoformans and Candida.
With caspofungin in oesophageal candidiasis, and with terbinafine in onychomycosis
Neither pairing appears in the lecture.
With griseofulvin in tinea capitis, and with nystatin in oral candidiasis
Those are dermatophyte and topical indications unrelated to flucytosine.
With voriconazole in invasive aspergillosis, and with fluconazole in vaginal candidiasis
The stated combinations are with amphotericin B and with itraconazole.

C.io: 1 — Identify dermatologic drug classes and commonly prescribed dermatologic drugs
C.q: Which conditions make up the atopic triad the lecture places atopic dermatitis within?
opts: Asthma and allergic rhino-conjunctivitis
Correct, and skin barrier dysfunction is what the lecture says plays the major role in the skin component.
Psoriasis and seborrhoeic dermatitis
Neither is part of the atopic triad as the lecture defines it.
Urticaria and angio-oedema
These are not the two conditions named.
Acne vulgaris and rosacea
These belong to the acne section of the lecture.

D.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
D.q: Which systemic effects does the lecture attribute to topical corticosteroids?
opts: Adrenal suppression, infections, hyperglycaemia, glaucoma, cataracts and growth retardation in children
Correct. That a topical agent can do all of this is the point of the potency and duration warnings.
